entries.23f124bad8ecd80f6e30466d6cf91d7dbcf89d75: <div sID="gen20615" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Hab.3" sID="Hab.3"/> <div eID="gen20615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20616" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20617" type="x-p"/> Still the correspondence is kept up between God and his prophet. In the <reference osisRef="Hab.1.1-Hab.1.17">first chapter</reference> he spoke to God, then God to him, and then he to God again; in the <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1-Hab.2.20">second chapter</reference> God spoke wholly to him by the Spirit of prophecy; now, in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.1-Hab.3.19">this chapter</reference>, he speaks wholly to God by the Spirit of prayer, for he would not let the intercourse drop on his side, like a genuine son of Abraham, who "returned not to his place until God had left communing with him." <reference osisRef="Gen.18.33">Gen. xviii. 33</reference>. The prophet's prayer, in this chapter, is in imitation of David's psalms, for it is directed "to the chief musician," and is set to musical instruments. The prayer is left upon record for the use of the church, and particularly of the Jews in their captivity, while they were waiting for their deliverance, promised by the vision in the foregoing chapter. I. He earnestly begs of God to relieve and succour his people in affliction, to hasten their deliverance, and to comfort them in the mean time, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.1">ver. 2</reference>. II. He calls to mind the experiences which the church formerly had of God's glorious and gracious appearances on her behalf, when he brought Israel out of Egypt through the wilderness to Canaan, and there many a time wrought wonderful deliverances for them, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.3-Hab.3.15">ver. 3-15</reference>. III. He affects himself with a holy concern for the present troubles of the church, but encourages himself and others to hope that the issue will be comfortable and glorious at last, though all visible means fail, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16-Hab.3.19">ver. 16-19</reference>.
entries.2f8c7c2ecd7c99c739551a8fd335b0e3255f5146: <div eID="gen20617" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20616" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet's Prayer. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20618" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth. <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , I have heard thy speech, <hi type="italic">and</hi> was afraid: <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy. <div eID="gen20618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20619" type="x-p"/> This chapter is entitled <hi type="italic">a prayer of Habakkuk.</hi> It is a meditation with himself, an intercession for the church. Prophets were praying men; this prophet was so (<hi type="italic">He is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen. xx. 7</reference>); and sometimes they prayed for even those whom they prophesied against. Those that were intimately acquainted with the mind of God concerning future events knew better than others how to order their prayers, and what to pray for, and, in the foresight of troublous times, could lay up a stock of prayers that might then receive a gracious answer, and so be serving the church by their prayers when their prophesying was over. This prophet had found God ready to answer his requests and complaints before, and therefore now repeats his applications to him. Because <hi type="italic">God has inclined his ear to us,</hi> we must resolve that <hi type="italic">therefore we</hi> will <hi type="italic">call upon him as long as we live.</hi> 1. The prophet owns the receipt of God's answer to his former representation, and the impression it made upon him (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Lord! I have heard thy speech, thy hearing</hi>" (so some read it), "that which thou wouldst have us hear, the decree that has gone forth for the afflicting of thy people. <hi type="italic">I received thine,</hi> and it is before me." Note, Those that would rightly order their speech to God must carefully observe, and lay before them, his speech to them. He had said (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">ch. ii. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will watch to see what he will say;</hi> and now he owns, <hi type="italic">Lord, I have heard thy speech;</hi> for, if we turn a deaf ear to God's word, we can expect no other than that he should turn a deaf ear to our prayers, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Prov. xxviii. 9</reference>. I heard it, <hi type="italic">and was afraid.</hi> Messages immediately from heaven commonly struck even the best and boldest men into a consternation; Moses, Isaiah, and Daniel, did <hi type="italic">exceedingly fear and quake.</hi> But, besides that, the matter of this message made the prophet afraid, when he heard how low the people of God should be brought, under the oppressing power of the Chaldeans, and how long they should continue under it; he was afraid lest their spirits should quite fail, and lest the church should be utterly rooted out and run down, and, being kept low so long, should be lost at length. 2. He earnestly prays that <hi type="italic">for the elect's sake</hi> these <hi type="italic">days of trouble</hi> might be <hi type="italic">shortened,</hi> or the trouble of these days mitigated and moderated, or the people of God supported and comforted under it. He thinks it very long to wait till the <hi type="italic">end of the years;</hi> perhaps he refers to the seventy years fixed for the continuance of the captivity, and therefore, "Lord," says he, "do something on our behalf <hi type="italic">in the midst of the years,</hi> those years of our distress; though we be not delivered, and our oppressors destroyed, yet let us not be abandoned and cast off." (1.) "Do something for thy own cause: <hi type="italic">Revive thy work,</hi> thy church" (that is the <hi type="italic">work of God's own hand,</hi> formed by him, formed for him); "<hi type="italic">revive</hi> that, even when it <hi type="italic">walks in the midst of trouble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.138.7-Ps.138.8">Ps. cxxxviii. 7, 8</reference>. Grant thy people <hi type="italic">a little reviving in their bondage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezra ix. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.6">Ps. lxxxv. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Preserve alive thy work</hi>" (so some read it); "though thy church be chastened, let it not be killed; though it have not its liberty, yet continue its life, save a remnant alive, to be a seed of another generation. <hi type="italic">Revive the work of thy grace</hi> in us, by sanctifying the trouble to us and supporting us under it, though the time be not yet come, <hi type="italic">even the set time,</hi> for our deliverance out of it. Whatever becomes of us, though we be as dead and dry bones, Lord, let <hi type="italic">thy work be revived,</hi> let not that sink, and go back, and come to nothing." (2.) "Do something for thy own honour: <hi type="italic">In the midst of the years make known,</hi> make thyself known, for now <hi type="italic">verily thou art a God that hidest thyself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa. xlv. 15</reference>), make known thy power, thy pity, thy promise, thy providence, in the government of the world, for the safety and welfare of thy church. Though we be buried in obscurity, yet, Lord, make thyself known; whatever becomes of Israel, let not the God of Israel be forgotten in the world, but discover himself even in the midst of the dark years, before thou art expected to appear." When <hi type="italic">in the midst of the years</hi> of the captivity God miraculously owned the three children in the fiery furnace, and humbled Nebuchadnezzar, this prayer was answered, <hi type="italic">In the midst of the years make known.</hi> (3.) "Do something for thy people's comfort: <hi type="italic">In wrath remember mercy,</hi> and <hi type="italic">make that known. Show us thy mercy, O Lord!</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.85.7">Ps. lxxxv. 7</reference>. They see God's displeasure against them in their troubles, and that makes them grievous indeed. There is wrath in the bitter cup; that therefore they deprecate, and are earnest in begging that he is a merciful God and they are vessels of his mercy. Note, Even those that are under the tokens of God's wrath must not despair of his mercy; and mercy, mere mercy, is that which we must flee to for refuge, and rely upon as our only plea. He does not say, Remember our merit, but, Lord, <hi type="italic">remember thy own mercy.</hi>
entries.ba495f36e7aec2a1bf38b32753fff2314fda89f5: <div eID="gen20619" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Majesty; Wonders Wrought for Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20620" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. <hi type="super">4</hi> And <hi type="italic">his</hi> brightness was as the light; he had horns <hi type="italic">coming</hi> out of his hand: and there <hi type="italic">was</hi> the hiding of his power. <hi type="super">5</hi> Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals went forth at his feet. <hi type="super">6</hi> He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways <hi type="italic">are</hi> everlasting. <hi type="super">7</hi> I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: <hi type="italic">and</hi> the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble. <hi type="super">8</hi> Was the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> displeased against the rivers? <hi type="italic">was</hi> thine anger against the rivers? <hi type="italic">was</hi> thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy chariots of salvation? <hi type="super">9</hi> Thy bow was made quite naked, <hi type="italic">according</hi> to the oaths of the tribes, <hi type="italic">even thy</hi> word. Selah. Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers. <hi type="super">10</hi> The mountains saw thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, <hi type="italic">and</hi> lifted up his hands on high. <hi type="super">11</hi> The sun <hi type="italic">and</hi> moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, <hi type="italic">and</hi> at the shining of thy glittering spear. <hi type="super">12</hi> Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, <hi type="italic">even</hi> for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou didst strike through with his staves the head of his villages: they came out as a whirlwind to scatter me: their rejoicing <hi type="italic">was</hi> as to devour the poor secretly. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses, <hi type="italic">through</hi> the heap of great waters. <div eID="gen20620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20621" type="x-p"/> It has been the usual practice of God's people, when they have been in distress and ready to fall into despair, to help themselves by recollecting their experiences, and reviving them, <hi type="italic">considering the days of old,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the years of ancient times</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.5">Ps. lxxvii. 5</reference>), and pleading with God in prayer, as he is pleased sometimes to plead them with himself. <reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">Isa. lxiii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Then he remembered the days of old.</hi> This is that which the prophet does here, and he looks as far back as the first forming of them into a people, when they were brought by miracles out of Egypt, <hi type="italic">a house of bondage,</hi> through the wilderness, <hi type="italic">a land of drought,</hi> into Canaan, then possessed by <hi type="italic">mighty nations.</hi> He that thus brought them at first into Canaan, through so much difficulty, can now bring them thither again out of Babylon, how great soever the difficulties are that lie in the way. Those works of wonder, wrought of old, are here most magnificently described, for the greater encouragement to the faith of God's people in their present straits. <div eID="gen20621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20622" type="x-p"/> I. God appeared in his glory, so as he never did before or since (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.3-Hab.3.4">v. 3, 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He came from Teman, even the Holy One from Mount Paran.</hi> This refers to the visible display of the glory of God when he gave the law upon Mount Sinai, as appears by <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deut. xxxiii. 2</reference> whence these expressions are borrowed. Then <hi type="italic">the Lord came down</hi> upon Mount Sinai in a cloud (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.20">Exod. xix. 20</reference>) and his glory was <hi type="italic">as the devouring fire,</hi> not only to enforce the law he then gave them, but to avow the deliverance he had wrought for them and to magnify it; for the first word he said there was, "<hi type="italic">I am the Lord thy God, that brought thee out of the land of Egypt.</hi> I that appear in this glory am the author of that work." Then <hi type="italic">his glory covered the heavens,</hi> which shone with the reflection of that glorious appearance of his; the <hi type="italic">earth also</hi> was <hi type="italic">full of his praise,</hi> or of his <hi type="italic">splendour,</hi> as some read it. People at a distance saw the cloud and fire on the top of Mount Sinai, and praised the God of Israel. Or the earth was full of those works of God which were to be praised. <hi type="italic">His brightness was as the light,</hi> as the light of the sun when he goes forth in his strength; <hi type="italic">he had horns,</hi> or <hi type="italic">bright beams</hi> (so it should be rendered), <hi type="italic">coming out of his side</hi> or <hi type="italic">hand.</hi> Rays of glory were darted forth around him; and with some rays borrowed thence it was that Moses's face shone when he <hi type="italic">came down from</hi> that <hi type="italic">mount</hi> of glory. Some by the horns, the <hi type="italic">two horns</hi> (for the word is dual), <hi type="italic">coming out of his hand,</hi> understand the <hi type="italic">two tables of the law,</hi> which perhaps, when God delivered them to Moses, though they were tables of stone, had a glory round them; those books were gilt with beams, and so it agrees with <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deut. xxxiii. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">From his right hand went a fiery law for them.</hi> It is added, <hi type="italic">And there was the hiding of his power;</hi> there was his hidden power, in the rays that came out of his hand. The operations of his power, compared with what he could have done, were rather the hiding of it than the discovery of it; the secrets of his power, as well as of his wisdom, are <hi type="italic">double to that which is,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job xi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen20622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20623" type="x-p"/> II. God sent plagues on Egypt, for the humbling of proud Pharaoh, and the obliging of him to let the people go (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Before him went the pestilence,</hi> which slew all the first-born of Egypt in one night; and <hi type="italic">burning coals went forth at his feet,</hi> when, in the plague of hail, there was <hi type="italic">fire mingled with hail—burning diseases</hi> (so the margin reads it), some think those that wasted Egypt, others those with which the number of the Canaanites was diminished before Israel was brought in up on them. These were <hi type="italic">at his feet,</hi> that is, at his coming, for they are at his command; he says to them, Go, and they go, Come, and they come, Do this, and they do it. <div eID="gen20623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20624" type="x-p"/> III. He divided the land of Canaan to his people Israel, and expelled the heathen from before them (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">He stood, and measured the earth,</hi> measured that land, to assign it for an inheritance to Israel his people, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.8-Deut.32.9">Deut. xxxii. 8, 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">He beheld, and drove asunder the nations</hi> that were in possession of it; though they combined together against Israel, God dispersed and discomfited them before Israel. Or he exerted such a mighty power as was enough to shake in pieces all the nations of the earth. Then <hi type="italic">the everlasting mountains were scattered, and the perpetual hills did bow;</hi> the mighty princes and potentates of Canaan, that seemed as high, as strong, and as firmly fixed, as the mountains and hills, were broken to pieces; they and their kingdoms were totally subdued. Or the power of God was so exerted as to shake the mountains and hills; nay, and Sinai did tremble, and the adjacent hills; see <reference osisRef="Ps.68.7-Ps.68.8">Ps. lxviii. 7, 8</reference>. To this he adds, <hi type="italic">His ways are everlasting,</hi> that is, all the motions of his providence are according to his eternal counsels; and he is the same for ever, that which he was yesterday and to-day. His covenant is unchangeable, and <hi type="italic">his mercy endures for ever.</hi> When he <hi type="italic">drove asunder the nations of Canaan</hi> one might have seen the <hi type="italic">tents of Cushan in affliction, the curtains of the land of Midian trembling,</hi> and all the inhabitants of the neighbouring countries taking the alarm; and though they were not in the commission given to Israel to destroy, nor their land within the warrant given to Israel to possess, yet they thought their own house in danger when their neighbour's house was on fire, and therefore they were in a great fright, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.7">v. 7</reference>. Balak the king of Moab was so, <reference osisRef="Num.22.3-Num.22.4">Num. xxii. 3, 4</reference>. Some make the tents of Cushan to be in affliction when, in the days of judge Othniel, God delivered Cushan-rishathaim into his hand (<reference osisRef="Judg.3.8">Judg. iii. 8</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">curtains of the land of Midian to tremble</hi> when, in the days of judge Gideon, a barley cake, in a dream, overthrew the tent of Midian, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.13">Judg. vii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen20624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20625" type="x-p"/> IV. He divided the Red Sea and Jordan, when they stood in the way of Israel's progress, and yet fetched a river out of a rock when Israel wanted it, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.8">v. 8</reference>. One would have thought that God was <hi type="italic">displeased with the rivers,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">his wrath</hi> was <hi type="italic">against the sea,</hi> for he made them give way and flee before him when he <hi type="italic">rode upon his horses and chariots of salvation,</hi> as a general at the head of his forces, mighty to save. Note, God's chariots are not so much chariots of state to himself as chariots of salvation to his people; it is his glory to be Israel's Saviour. This seems to be referred to again (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou didst walk through the sea,</hi> through the Red Sea, <hi type="italic">with thy horses,</hi> in the pillar of cloud and fire (that was his chariot drawn by angels); thus thou didst walk secure, and so as to accommodate thyself to the slow pace that Israel could go, as Jacob tenderly drove, in consideration of his children and cattle: <hi type="italic">Thou didst walk through the heap,</hi> or mud, <hi type="italic">of great waters;</hi> and Israel likewise was led <hi type="italic">through the deep as a horse through the wilderness,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.63.13-Isa.63.14">Isa. lxiii. 13, 14</reference>. When they came to enter Canaan the <hi type="italic">overflowing of the water passed by,</hi> that is, Jordan, which at that time overflowed all his banks, was divided, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.15">Jos. iii. 15</reference>. Note, When the difficulties in the way of perfecting the salvation of Israel seem most insuperable, when they rise to the height, and overflow, yet then God can put them by, break through them, and get over them. Then <hi type="italic">the deep uttered his voice,</hi> when, the Red Sea and Jordan being divided, the waters roared and made a noise, as if they were sensible of the restraint they were under from proceeding in their natural course, and complained of it. They <hi type="italic">lifted up their hands,</hi> or sides, <hi type="italic">on high</hi> (for the waters <hi type="italic">stood up on a heap,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.3.16">Jos. iii. 16</reference>), as if they would have made opposition to the orders given them. They <hi type="italic">lifted up their voice, lifted up their waves;</hi> but in vain. <hi type="italic">The Lord on high was mightier than they,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4">Ps. xciii. 3, 4</reference>. With the dividing of the sea and Jordan, notice is again taken of the trembling of the mountains, as if the stop given to the waters gave a shock to the adjacent hills; they are put together, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.3-Ps.114.4">Ps. cxiv. 3, 4</reference>. When <hi type="italic">the sea saw it and fled,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jordan was driven back, the mountains skipped like rams and the little hills like lambs.</hi> The whole creation yielded; earth and waters trembled <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the mighty God of Jacob.</hi> But (as Mr. Cowley paraphrases it) <div eID="gen20625" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen20626"/> <l level="1" sID="gen20627"/>Fly where thou wilt, thou sea; and, Jordan's current, cease.<l eID="gen20627" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen20628"/>Jordan, there is no need of thee;<l eID="gen20628" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen20629"/>For at God's word, whene'er he please,<l eID="gen20629" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen20630"/>The rocks shall weep new waters forth instead of these.<l eID="gen20630" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen20626"/> <div sID="gen20631" type="x-p"/> So here, <hi type="italic">Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers;</hi> channels were made in the wilderness, such as seemed to cleave the earth, for the waters to run in, which issued out of the rock, to supply the camp of Israel, and which followed them in all their removes. Note, The God of nature can alter and control the powers of nature, which way he pleases, can turn waters into crystal rocks and rocks into crystal streams. <div eID="gen20631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20632" type="x-p"/> V. He arrested the motion of the sun and moon, to befriend and complete Israel's victories (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sun and moon stood still</hi> at the prayer of Joshua, that the Canaanites might not have the benefit of the night to favour their escape; they <hi type="italic">stood still in their habitation</hi> in the heaven (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.4">Ps. xix. 4</reference>), but with an eye to Gibeon and the <hi type="italic">valley of Ajalon,</hi> where God's work was in the doing, and of which they, though at so vast a distance, attended the motions. <hi type="italic">At the light,</hi> at the direction, <hi type="italic">of thy arrows, they went,</hi> and at <hi type="italic">the shining of thy glittering spear;</hi> they followed Israel's arms, to favour them; according to the intimation of the arrows God shot (as Jonathan's arrows, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.20">1 Sam. xx. 20</reference>), and which way soever his spear pointed (the glittering light of which they acknowledged to outshine theirs) that way they directed their influences, benign to Israel and malignant against their enemies, as when <hi type="italic">the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.</hi> Note, The heavenly bodies, as well as earth and seas, are at God's command, and, when he pleases, at Israel's service too. <div eID="gen20632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20633" type="x-p"/> VI. He carried on and completed Israel's victories over the nations of Canaan and their kings; he <hi type="italic">slew great kings</hi> and <hi type="italic">famous,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.136.17-Ps.136.18">Ps. cxxxvi. 17, 18</reference>. This is largely insisted upon here, as a proper plea with God to enforce the present petition, that he would restore them again to that land which they were, at the expense of so many lives, so many miracles, first put in possession of. <div eID="gen20633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20634" type="x-p"/> 1. Many expressions are here used to set forth the conquest of Canaan. (1.) God's <hi type="italic">bow was made quite naked,</hi> taken out of the case, to be employed for Israel; we should say, his <hi type="italic">sword was quite unsheathed,</hi> not drawn out a little way, to frighten the enemy, and then put up again, but quite drawn out, not to be returned till they are all cut off. (2.) He <hi type="italic">marched through the land</hi> from end to end, <hi type="italic">in indignation,</hi> as scorning to let that wicked generation of Canaanites any longer possess so good a land. He marched <hi type="italic">cum fastidio—with distaste</hi> (so some), despising their confederacies. (3.) He <hi type="italic">threshed the heathen in anger,</hi> trod them down, nay, he trod them out, as corn in the floor, to give them, and what they had, to be meat to his people Israel, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.13">Mic. iv. 13</reference>. (4.) He <hi type="italic">wounded the heads out of the house of the wicked;</hi> he destroyed the families of the Canaanites, and wounded their princes, the heads of their families; nay, he cut off the heads, and so <hi type="italic">discovered the foundations of them,</hi> even <hi type="italic">to the neck.</hi> Are they a building? They are razed even to the foundation. Are they a body? They are plunged into deep mire even to the neck, so that they cannot get out, or help themselves. He <hi type="italic">broke the heads of leviathan in pieces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Ps. lxxiv. 14</reference>. Some apply this to Christ's victories over Satan and the powers of darkness, in which he <hi type="italic">wounded the heads over many countries,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.6">Ps. cx. 6</reference>. (5.) He <hi type="italic">struck through with his staves the head of the villages</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.14">v. 14</reference>); with Israel's staves God <hi type="italic">struck through</hi> the <hi type="italic">head of the villages</hi> of the enemies, whether Egypt or Canaan. Staves shall do the same execution as swords when God pleases to make use of them. The enemy came out with the utmost force and fury, <hi type="italic">as a whirlwind to scatter me</hi> (says Israel); for <hi type="italic">many a time have they thus afflicted me,</hi> thus attacked me, <hi type="italic">from my youth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.129.1">Ps. cxxix. 1</reference>. Pharaoh, when he pursued Israel to the Red Sea, <hi type="italic">came out as a whirlwind;</hi> so did the kings of Canaan in their confederacies against Israel. <hi type="italic">Their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly;</hi> they were as confident of success in their enterprise as ever any great man was of devouring a poor man, that was no way a match for him; and his design against him was carried on with secrecy. But God disappointed them, and their pride did but make their fall the more shameful and God's care of his poor the more illustrious. (6.) He <hi type="italic">walked to the sea with his horses</hi> (so some read it, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.15">v. 15</reference>), that is, he carried Israel's victories to the Great Sea, which was opposite to that side of Canaan at which they entered, so that they went quite through it, and made themselves masters of it all, or rather God made them so, for they <hi type="italic">got it not by their own sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Ps. xliv. 3</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen20634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20635" type="x-p"/> 2. There were three things that God had a eye to, in giving Israel so many bloody victories over the Canaanites:—(1.) He would hereby make good his promise to the fathers; it was <hi type="italic">according to the oaths of the tribes, even his word,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.9">v. 9</reference>. He had sworn to give this land to the <hi type="italic">tribes of Israel;</hi> it was his oath <hi type="italic">to Isaac confirmed to Jacob,</hi> and repeated many a time to <hi type="italic">the tribes of Israel, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan.</hi> This word God will accomplish, though Israel be ever so unworthy (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.5">Deut. ix. 5</reference>) and their enemies ever so many and mighty. Note, What God does for his tribes is according to the oaths of the tribes, according to what he has said and sworn to them; <hi type="italic">for he is faithful that has promised.</hi> (2.) He would hereby show his kindness to <hi type="italic">his people,</hi> because of their relation to him, and his interest in them: <hi type="italic">Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">v. 13</reference>. All the powers of nature are shaken, and the course of nature changed, and every thing seems to be thrown into disorder, and all is <hi type="italic">for the salvation of God's people.</hi> There are a people in the world who are God's people, and their salvation is that which he has in his eye in all the operations of his providence. Heaven and earth shall sooner come together than any of the links in the golden chain of their salvation shall be broken; and even that which seems most unlikely shall by an overruling hand be made to work for their salvation, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.19">Phil. i. 19</reference>. (3.) He would hereby give a type and figure of the redemption of the world by Jesus Christ. It is <hi type="italic">for salvation with thy anointed,</hi> with Joshua, who led the armies of Israel and was a figure of him whose name he bore, even Jesus our Joshua. What God did for his Israel of old was done with an eye to his anointed, for the sake of the Mediator, who was both the founder and foundation of the covenant made with them. It was salvation <hi type="italic">with him,</hi> for in all the salvations wrought for them, <hi type="italic">God looked upon the face of the anointed,</hi> and did them by him.
entries.7bdb4f1c3190c9ca655cf7dd2b033380d0aafd04: <div eID="gen20635" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Conquest of Canaan; Devout Confidence. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20636" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> When I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble: when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade them with his troops. <hi type="super">17</hi> Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither <hi type="italic">shall</hi> fruit <hi type="italic">be</hi> in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> no herd in the stalls: <hi type="super">18</hi> Yet I will rejoice in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , I will joy in the God of my salvation. <hi type="super">19</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God <hi type="italic">is</hi> my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' <hi type="italic">feet,</hi> and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments. <div eID="gen20636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20637" type="x-p"/> Within the compass of these few lines we have the prophet in the highest degree both of trembling and triumphing, such are the varieties both of the state and of the spirit of God's people in this world. In heaven there shall be no more trembling, but everlasting triumphs. <div eID="gen20637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20638" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet had foreseen the prevalence of the church's enemies and the long continuance of the church's troubles; and the sight made him tremble, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16">v. 16</reference>. Here he goes on with what he had said <reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">v. 2</reference>, "<hi type="italic">I have heard thy speech and was afraid. When I heard</hi> what sad times were coming upon the church <hi type="italic">my belly trembled, my lips quivered at the voice;</hi> the news made such an impression that it put me into a perfect ague fit." The blood retiring to the heart, to succour that when it was ready to faint, the extreme parts were left destitute of spirits, so that <hi type="italic">his lips quivered.</hi> Nay, he was so weak, and so unable to help himself, that he was as if <hi type="italic">rottenness</hi> had <hi type="italic">entered into his bones;</hi> he had no strength left in him, could neither stand nor go; he <hi type="italic">trembled in himself,</hi> trembled all over him, trembled within him; he yielded to his trembling, and <hi type="italic">troubled himself,</hi> as our Savior did; his <hi type="italic">flesh trembled for fear of God</hi> and <hi type="italic">he was afraid of his judgments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.120">Ps. cxix. 120</reference>. He was touched with a tender concern for the calamities of the church, and trembled for fear lest they should end at length in ruin, and the <hi type="italic">name of Israel be blotted out.</hi> Nor did he think it any disparagement to him, nor any reproach to his courage, but freely owned he was one of those that <hi type="italic">trembled at God's word,</hi> for to them he will look with favour: <hi type="italic">I tremble in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble.</hi> Note, When we see a day of trouble approaching it concerns us to provide accordingly, and to lay up something in store, by the help of which we may rest in that day; and the best way to make sure rest for ourselves in the day of trouble is to tremble within ourselves at the word of God and the threatenings of that word. He that has joy in store for those that <hi type="italic">sow in tears</hi> has rest in store for those that tremble before him. <hi type="italic">Good hope through grace</hi> is founded in a <hi type="italic">holy fear.</hi> Noah, who was <hi type="italic">moved with fear,</hi> trembled within himself at the warning given him of the deluge coming, had the ark for his resting place in the day of that trouble. The prophet tells us what he said in his trembling. His fear is that, <hi type="italic">when he comes up to the people,</hi> when the <hi type="italic">Chaldean comes up to the people</hi> of Israel, <hi type="italic">he will invade them,</hi> will surround them, will break in upon them, nay (as it is in the margin), He will <hi type="italic">cut them in pieces with his troops;</hi> he cried out, We are all undone; the whole nation of the Jews is lost and gone. Note, When things look bad we are too apt to aggravate them, and make the worst of them. <div eID="gen20638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20639" type="x-p"/> II. He had looked back upon the experiences of the church in former ages, and had observed what great things God had done for them, and so he recovered himself out of his fright, and not only retrieved his temper, but fell into a transport of holy joy, with an express <hi type="italic">non obstante—notwithstanding</hi> to the calamities he foresaw coming, and this not for himself only, but in the name of every faithful Israelite. <div eID="gen20639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20640" type="x-p"/> 1. He supposes the ruin of all his creature comforts and enjoyments, not only of the delights of this life, but even of the necessary supports of it, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.17">v. 17</reference>. Famine is one of the ordinary effects of war, and those commonly feel it first and most that sit still and are quiet; the prophet and his pious friends, when the Chaldean army comes, will be plundered and stripped of all they have. Or he supposes himself deprived of all by blasting and unseasonable weather, or some other immediate hand of God. Or though the captives in Babylon have not that plenty of all good things in their own land. (1.) He supposes the fruit-tree to be withered and become barren; the <hi type="italic">fig-tree</hi> (which used to furnish them with much of their food; hence we often read of <hi type="italic">cakes of figs</hi>) shall not so much as <hi type="italic">blossom, nor shall fruit be in the vine,</hi> from which they had their drink, that made glad the heart: he supposes <hi type="italic">the labour of the olive</hi> to <hi type="italic">fail,</hi> their oil, which was to them as butter is to us; the <hi type="italic">labour of the olive shall lie</hi> (so it is in the margin); their expectations from it shall be disappointed. (2.) He supposes the bread-corn to fail; <hi type="italic">the fields shall yield no meat;</hi> and, since <hi type="italic">the king himself is served of the field,</hi> if the productions of that be withdrawn, every one will feel the want of them. (3.) He supposes the cattle to perish for want of the food which the field should yield and does not, or by disease, or being destroyed and carried away by the enemy: <hi type="italic">The flock is cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stall.</hi> Note, When we are in the full enjoyment of our creature comforts we should consider that there may come a time when we shall be stripped of them all, and use them accordingly, as not abusing them, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.29-1Cor.7.30">1 Cor. vii. 29, 30</reference>. <div eID="gen20640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20641" type="x-p"/> 2. He resolves to delight and triumph in God notwithstanding; when all is gone his God is not gone (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Yet will I rejoice in the Lord;</hi> I shall have him to rejoice in, and will rejoice in him." <hi type="italic">Destroy the vines and the fig-trees,</hi> and you make all the mirth of a carnal heart to cease, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.11-Hos.2.12">Hos. ii. 11, 12</reference>. But those who, when they were full, enjoyed God in all, when they are emptied and impoverished can <hi type="italic">enjoy all in God,</hi> and can sit down upon a melancholy heap of the ruins of all their creature comforts and even then can sing to the praise and glory of God, as the God of their salvation. This is the principal ground of our joy in God, that he is the God of our salvation, our eternal salvation, the salvation of the soul; and, if he be so, we may rejoice in him as such in our greatest distresses, since by them our salvation cannot be hindered, but may be furthered. Note, Joy in God is never out of season, nay, it is in a special manner seasonable when we meet with losses and crosses in the world, that it may then appear that our hearts are not set upon these things, nor our happiness bound up in them. See how the prophet triumphs in God: <hi type="italic">The Lord God is my strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">v. 19</reference>. He that is the <hi type="italic">God of our salvation</hi> in another world will be our strength in this world, to carry us on in our journey thither, and help us over the difficulties and oppositions we meet with in our way. Even when provisions are cut off, to make it appear that <hi type="italic">man lives not by bread alone,</hi> we may have the want of bread supplied by the graces and comforts of God's Spirit and with the supplies of them. (1.) We shall be strong for our spiritual warfare and work: <hi type="italic">The Lord God is my strength,</hi> the strength of my heart. (2.) We shall be swift for our spiritual race: "<hi type="italic">He will make my feet like hinds' feet,</hi> that with enlargement of heart I may run the way of his commands and outrun my troubles." (3.) We shall be successful in our spiritual enterprises: "<hi type="italic">He will make me to walk upon my high places;</hi> that is, I shall gain my point, shall be restored unto my own land, and tread upon the high places of the enemy," <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">Deut. xxxii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">xxxiii. 29</reference>. Thus the prophet, who began his prayer with fear and trembling, concludes it with joy and triumph, for prayer is heart's ease to a gracious soul. When Hannah had prayed she <hi type="italic">went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad.</hi> This prophet, finding it so, publishes his experience of it, and puts it into the hand of the <hi type="italic">chief singer</hi> for the use of the church, especially in the day of our captivity. And, though then the harps were hung upon the willow-trees, yet in the hope that they would be resumed, and their right hand retrieve its cunning, which it had forgotten, he set his song upon <hi type="italic">Shigionoth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.1">v. 1</reference>), wandering tunes, <hi type="italic">according to the variable songs,</hi> and upon <hi type="italic">Neginoth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">the stringed instruments.</hi> He that is afflicted, and has prayed aright, may then be so easy, may then be so merry, as to sing psalms.  <chapter eID="Hab.3"/> <div eID="gen20641" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen20564" osisID="Hab" type="book"/>

entries.951e9f76ac5d15058c277c96e18df5c649f8546b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12903"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hab.3.1-Hab.3.19">Ha 3:1-19</reference>. Habakkuk's Prayer to God: God's Glorious Revelation of Himself at Sinai and at Gibeon, a Pledge of His Interposing Again in Behalf of Israel against Babylon, and All Other Foes; Hence the Prophet's Confidence Amid Calamities.</title> <div sID="gen24102" type="x-p"/> This sublime ode begins with an exordium (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.1">Ha 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>), then follows the main subject, then the peroration (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.16-Hab.3.19">Ha 3:16-19</reference>), a summary of the practical truth, which the whole is designed to teach. (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.2-Deut.33.5">De 33:2-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.13-Ps.77.20">Psa 77:13-20</reference> are parallel odes). This was probably designed by the Spirit to be a fit formula of prayer for the people, first in their Babylonian exile, and now in their dispersion, especially towards the close of it, just before the great Deliverer is to interpose for them. It was used in public worship, as the musical term, "Selah!" (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.3">Ha 3:3</reference>, 9, 13), implies.<div eID="gen24102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12903"/><hi type="bold">1. prayer--</hi>the only strictly called prayers are in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">Ha 3:2</reference>. But all devotional addresses to God are called "prayers" (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.20">Psa 72:20</reference>). The Hebrew is from a root "to apply to a judge for a favorable decision." Prayers in which praises to God for deliverance, anticipated in the sure confidence of faith, are especially calculated to enlist Jehovah on His people's side (2Ch 20:20-22, 26).<div eID="gen24103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon Shigionoth--</hi>a musical phrase, "after the manner of elegies," or mournful odes, from an Arabic root [Lee]; the phrase is singular in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1">Psa 7:1</reference>, title. More simply, from a Hebrew root to "err," "on account of sins of ignorance." Habakkuk thus teaches his countrymen to confess not only their more grievous sins, but also their errors and negligences, into which they were especially likely to fall when in exile away from the Holy Land [Calvin]. So Vulgate and Aquila, and Symmachus. "For voluntary transgressors" [Jerome]. Probably the subject would regulate the kind of music. Delitzsch and Henderson translate, "With triumphal music," from the same root "to err," implying its enthusiastic irregularity. <div eID="gen24104" type="x-p"/>
entries.96677520bbfe51827ac41106092463d4b1988b1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12904"/><div sID="gen24105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12904"/><hi type="bold">2. I have heard thy speech--</hi>Thy revelation to me concerning the coming chastisement of the Jews [Calvin], and the destruction of their oppressors. This is Habakkuk's reply to God's communication [Grotius]. Maurer translates, "the report of Thy coming," literally, "Thy report."<div eID="gen24105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and was afraid--</hi>reverential fear of God's judgments (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.16">Ha 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen24106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">revive thy work--</hi>Perfect the work of delivering Thy people, and do not let Thy promise lie as if it were dead, but give it new life by performing it [Menochius]. Calvin explains "thy work" to be Israel; called "the work of My hands" (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.11">Is 45:11</reference>). God's elect people are peculiarly His work (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Is 43:1</reference>), pre-eminently illustrating His power, wisdom, and goodness. "Though we seem, as it were, dead nationally, revive us" (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.6">Psa 85:6</reference>). However (<reference osisRef="Ps.64.9">Psa 64:9</reference>), where "the work of God" refers to His judgment on their enemies, favors the former view (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.16">Psa 90:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Is 51:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen24107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst of the years--</hi>namely, of calamity in which we live. Now that our calamities are at their height; during our seventy years' captivity. Calvin more fancifully explains it, in the midst of the years of Thy people, extending from Abraham to Messiah; if they be cut off before His coming, they will be cut off as it were in the midst of their years, before attaining their maturity. So Bengel makes the midst of the years to be the middle point of the years of the world. There is a strikingly similar phrase (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>), In the midst of the week. The parallel clause, "in wrath" (that is, in the midst of wrath), however, shows that "in the midst of the years" means "in the years of our present exile and calamity."<div eID="gen24108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make known--</hi>Made it (Thy work) known by experimental proof; show in very deed, that this is Thy work. <div eID="gen24109" type="x-p"/>
entries.767c16ea83451be180078a1ea1ce7bc7799f352b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12905"/><div sID="gen24110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12905"/><hi type="bold">3. God--</hi>singular in the Hebrew, "Eloah," instead of "Elohim," plural, usually employed. The singular is not found in any other of the minor prophets, or Jeremiah, or Ezekiel; but it is in Isaiah, Daniel, Job, and Deuteronomy.<div eID="gen24110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Teman--</hi>the country south of Judea and near Edom, in which latter country Mount Paran was situated [Henderson]. "Paran" is the desert region, extending from the south of Judah to Sinai. Seir, Sinai, and Paran are adjacent to one another, and are hence associated together, in respect to God's giving of the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">De 33:2</reference>). Teman is so identified with Seir or Edom, as here to be substituted for it. Habakkuk appeals to God's glorious manifestations to His people at Sinai, as the ground for praying that God will "revive His work" (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">Ha 3:2</reference>) now. For He is the same God now as ever.<div eID="gen24111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Selah--</hi>a musical sign, put at the close of sections and strophes, always at the end of a verse, except thrice; namely, here, and <reference osisRef="Hab.3.9">Ha 3:9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">57:3</reference>, where, however, it closes the hemistich. It implies a change of the modulation. It comes from a root to "rest" or "pause" [Gesenius]; implying a cessation of the chant, during an instrumental interlude. The solemn pause here prepares the mind for contemplating the glorious description of Jehovah's manifestation which follows.<div eID="gen24112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earth ... full of his praise--</hi>that is, of His glories which were calculated to call forth universal praise; the parallelism to "glory" proves this to be the sense. <div eID="gen24113" type="x-p"/>
entries.9812690e4a25d7f81c0d2b2b48ee42a068b1c0a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12906"/><div sID="gen24114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12906"/><hi type="bold">4. as the light--</hi>namely, of the sun (<reference osisRef="Job.37.21">Job 37:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen24114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horns--</hi>the emblem of power wielded by "His hand" [Ludovicus De Dieu]. "Rays" emanating from "His hand," compared by the Arabs to the horns of the gazelle (compare "hind of the morning," <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1">Psa 22:1</reference>, title, Margin). The Hebrew verb for to "emit rays," is from the root meaning "horns" (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.29">Ex 34:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.35">30, 35</reference>) [Grotius]. The rays are His lightnings (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.8">Psa 18:8</reference>), [Maurer].<div eID="gen24115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there--</hi>in that "brightness." In it, notwithstanding its brilliancy, there was but the veil "(the hiding) of His power." Even "light," God's "garment," covers, instead of revealing fully, His surpassing glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>) [Henderson]. Or, on Mount Sinai [Drusius]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.24.17">Ex 24:17</reference>). The Septuagint and Syriac versions read for "there," He made a hiding, &c.; He hid Himself with clouds. English Version is better, which Calvin explains, there is said to be "a hiding of God's power," because God did not reveal it indiscriminately to all, but specially to His people (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>). The contrast seems to me to be between the "horns" or emanations out of His power ("hand"), and that "power" itself. The latter was hidden, whereas the "horns" or emanations alone were manifested. If the mere scintillations were so awfully overwhelming, how much more so the hidden power itself! This was especially true of His manifestation at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Is 45:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen24116" type="x-p"/>
entries.35df4d0d869e57c7bf2eee2ac7333ddc64d7ae34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12907"/><div sID="gen24117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12907"/><hi type="bold">5. pestilence--</hi>to destroy His people's foes (<reference osisRef="1Sam.5.9">1Sa 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.11">11</reference>). As Jehovah's advent is glorious to His people, so it is terrible to His foes.<div eID="gen24117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burning coals--</hi><reference osisRef="Ps.18.8">Psa 18:8</reference> favors English Version. But the parallelism requires, as the Margin translates, "burning disease" (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.24">De 32:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.6">Psa 91:6</reference>).<div eID="gen24118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went ... at his feet--</hi>that is, after Him, as His attendants (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.10">Jud 4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen24119" type="x-p"/>
entries.1fcdb66037ce45390b36ced459a7aa221477cda6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12908"/><div sID="gen24120" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12908"/><hi type="bold">6. He stood, and measured the earth--</hi>Jehovah, in His advance, is represented as stopping suddenly, and measuring the earth with His all-seeing glance, whereat there is universal consternation. Maurer, from a different root, translates, "rocked the earth"; which answers better to the parallel "drove asunder"; the Hebrew for which latter, however, may be better translated, "made to tremble."<div eID="gen24120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting mountains--</hi>which have ever been remembered as retaining the same place and form from the foundation of the world.<div eID="gen24121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">did bow--</hi>as it were, in reverent submission.<div eID="gen24122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his ways are everlasting--</hi>His marvellous ways of working for the salvation of His people mark His everlasting character: such as He was in His workings for them formerly, such shall He be now. <div eID="gen24123" type="x-p"/>
entries.05b99bc318f71e614d793474707740c1cf66c016: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12909"/><div sID="gen24124" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12909"/><hi type="bold">7. the tents--</hi>that is, the dwellers.<div eID="gen24124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Cushan--</hi>the same as Cush; made "Cush-an" to harmonize with "Midi-an" in the parallel clause. So Lotan is found in the Hebrew of Genesis for Lot. Bochart therefore considers it equivalent to Midian, or a part of Arabia. So in <reference osisRef="Num.12.1">Nu 12:1</reference>, Moses' Midianite wife is called an Ethiopian (Hebrew, Cushite). Maurer thinks the dwellers on both sides of the Arabian Gulf, or Red Sea, are meant; for in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Ha 3:6</reference> God's everlasting or ancient ways of delivering His people are mentioned; and in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.8">Ha 3:8</reference>, the dividing of the Red Sea for them. Compare Miriam's song as to the fear of Israel's foes far and near caused thereby (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.14-Exod.15.16">Ex 15:14-16</reference>). Hebrew expositors refer it to Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, or Syria, the first oppressor of Israel (<reference osisRef="Judg.3.8">Jud 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.3.10">10</reference>), from whom Othniel delivered them. Thus the second hemistich of the verse will refer to the deliverance of Israel from Midian by Gideon (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.1-Judg.7.25">Jud 6:1-7:25</reference>) to which <reference osisRef="Hab.3.11">Ha 3:11</reference> plainly refers. Whichever of these views be correct, the general reference is to God's interpositions against Israel's foes of old.<div eID="gen24125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in affliction--</hi>rather, "under affliction" (regarded) as a heavy burden. Literally, "vanity" or "iniquity," hence the punishment of it (compare <reference osisRef="Num.25.17">Nu 25:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.25.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen24126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">curtains--</hi>the coverings of their tents; the shifting habitations of the nomad tribes, which resembled the modern Bedouins.<div eID="gen24127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tremble--</hi>namely, at Jehovah's terrible interposition for Israel against them. <div eID="gen24128" type="x-p"/>
entries.df113cb560e22169e4cf0d1ea4537db9d033f207: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12910"/><div sID="gen24129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12910"/><hi type="bold">8. Was the Lord displeased against the rivers?--</hi>"Was the cause of His dividing the Red Sea and Jordan His displeasure against these waters?" The answer to this is tacitly implied in "Thy chariots of salvation." "Nay; it was not displeasure against the waters, but His pleasure in interposing for His people's salvation" (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">Ha 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen24129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy chariots--</hi>in antithesis to Thy foe, Pharaoh's chariots," which, notwithstanding their power and numbers, were engulfed in the waters of destruction. God can make the most unlikely means work for His people's salvation (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.7">Ex 14:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.23">9, 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.25-Exod.9.28">25-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.3-Exod.15.8">15:3-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.19">19</reference>). Jehovah's chariots are His angels (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>), or the cherubim, or the ark (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.13">Jos 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.4.7">4:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Song.1.9">So 1:9</reference>). <div eID="gen24130" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce4ec16d1f2c55a675605c6c0dc36c9b00702ce5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12911"/><div sID="gen24131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12911"/><hi type="bold">9. bow ... made ... naked--</hi>that is, was drawn forth from its cover, in which bows usually were cased when not in use. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>, "Kir uncovered the shield."<div eID="gen24131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the oaths of the tribes even thy word--</hi>that is, Thy oaths of promise to the tribes of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.8">Psa 77:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.73">Lu 1:73</reference>, 74). Habakkuk shows that God's miraculous interpositions for His people were not limited to one time, but that God's oaths to His people are sure ground for their always expecting them. The mention of the tribes, rather than Abraham or Moses, is in order that they may not doubt that to them belongs this grace of which Abraham was the depository [Calvin and Jerome]. Maurer translates, "The spears were glutted with blood, the triumphal song!" that is, no sooner did Jehovah begin the battle by baring His bow, than the spears were glutted with blood and the triumphal song sung.<div eID="gen24132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers--</hi>the result of the earthquake caused by God's approach [Maurer]. Grotius refers it to the bringing forth water from the rock (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.6">Ex 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.20.10">Nu 20:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.20.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.15">Psa 78:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.4">105:4</reference>). But the context implies not the giving of water to His people to drink, but the fearful physical phenomena attending Jehovah's attack on Israel's foes. <div eID="gen24133" type="x-p"/>
entries.968186f09d7b7fa4b99f502d9b4b1e50e47ba6e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12912"/><div sID="gen24134" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12912"/><hi type="bold">10. The mountains--</hi>repetition with increased emphasis of some of the tremendous phenomena mentioned in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Ha 3:6</reference>.<div eID="gen24134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overflowing of the water passed by--</hi>namely, of the Red Sea; and again, of the Jordan. God marked His favor to His people in all the elements, causing every obstacle, whether mountains or waters, which impeded their progress, to "pass away" [Calvin]. Maurer, not so well, translates, "torrents (rains) of water rush down."<div eID="gen24135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lifted ... hands on high--</hi>namely, its billows lifted on high by the tempest. Personification. As men signify by voice or gesture of hand that they will do what they are commanded, so these parts of nature testified their obedience to God's will (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.22">Ex 14:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.3.16">Jos 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.17">Psa 77:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">114:4</reference>). <div eID="gen24136" type="x-p"/>
entries.5cb5e6edc95d387b14f8f5b3aa739f9367b3e1b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12913"/><div sID="gen24137" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12913"/><hi type="bold">11. sun ... moon stood still--</hi>at Joshua's command (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.12">Jos 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.13">13</reference>). Maurer wrongly translates, "stand" (withdrawn, or hidden from view, by the clouds which covered the sky during the thunders).<div eID="gen24137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">light of thine arrows--</hi>hail mixed with lightnings (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen24138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they went--</hi>The sun and moon "went," not as always heretofore, but according to the light and direction of Jehovah's arrows, namely, His lightnings hurled in defense of His people; astonished at these they stood still [Calvin]. Maurer translates, "At the light of Thine arrows (which) went" or flew. <div eID="gen24139" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3f8001d269b375939870dd157767a8becb645eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12914"/><div sID="gen24140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12914"/><hi type="bold">12. march--</hi>implying Jehovah's majestic and irresistible progress before His people (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.4">Jud 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.7">Psa 68:7</reference>). Israel would not have dared to attack the nations, unless Jehovah had gone before.<div eID="gen24140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thresh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Mic.4.13">Mi 4:13</reference>). <div eID="gen24141" type="x-p"/>
entries.3055f75f7427b7780449409f138f9f29b024fb4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12915"/><div sID="gen24142" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12915"/><hi type="bold">13. with thine anointed--</hi>with Messiah; of whom Moses, Joshua, and David, God's anointed leaders of Israel, were the types (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.19">Psa 89:19</reference>, 20, 38). God from the beginning delivered His people in person, or by the hand of a Mediator (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">Is 63:11</reference>). Thus Habakkuk confirms believers in the hope of their deliverance, as well because God is always the same, as also because the same anointed Mediator is ready now to fulfil God's will and interpose for Israel, as of old [Calvin]. Maurer translates to suit the parallelism, "for salvation to Thine anointed," namely, Israel's king in the abstract, answering to the "people" in the former clause (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.28.8">Psa 28:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">La 4:20</reference>). Or Israel is meant, the anointed, that is, consecrated people of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.15">Psa 105:15</reference>).<div eID="gen24142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24143" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked--</hi>probably an allusion to <reference osisRef="Ps.68.21">Psa 68:21</reference>. Each head person sprung from and belonging to the house of Israel's wicked foes; such as Jabin, whose city Hazor was "the head of all the kingdoms" of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.10">Jos 11:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Judg.4.2">Jud 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.3.13">3, 13</reference>).<div eID="gen24143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">discovering the foundation--</hi>Thou destroyedst high and low. As "the head of the house" means the prince, so the "foundation" means the general host of the enemy.<div eID="gen24144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the neck--</hi>image from a flood reaching to the neck (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.28">30:28</reference>). So God, by His wrath overflowing on the foe, caused their princes' necks to be trodden under foot by Israel's leaders (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">Jos 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.11.8">11:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen24145" type="x-p"/>
entries.70b5880107756892d21aeb286d47740b2d0cece2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12916"/><div sID="gen24146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12916"/><hi type="bold">14. strike ... with his staves--</hi>with the "wicked" (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">Ha 3:13</reference>) foe's own sword (Maurer translates, "spears") (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.22">Jud 7:22</reference>).<div eID="gen24146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">head of his villages--</hi>Not only kings were overthrown by God's hand, but His vengeance passed through the foe's villages and dependencies. A just retribution, as the foe had made "the inhabitants of Israel's villages to cease" (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.7">Jud 5:7</reference>). Grotius translates, "of his warriors"; Gesenius, "the chief of his captains."<div eID="gen24147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to scatter me--</hi>Israel, with whom Habakkuk identifies himself (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.1.12">Ha 1:12</reference>).<div eID="gen24148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoicing ... to devour the poor secretly--</hi>"The poor" means the Israelites, for whom in their helpless state the foe lurks in his lair, like a wild beast, to pounce on and devour (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.9">Psa 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.12">17:12</reference>). <div eID="gen24149" type="x-p"/>
entries.71cfde66b16c2d2ec00ab46e5ef0ea760be5aea4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12917"/><div sID="gen24150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12917"/><hi type="bold">15. Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hab.3.8">Ha 3:8</reference>). No obstacle could prevent Thy progress when leading Thy people in safety to their inheritance, whether the Red Sea, Jordan, or the figurative waves of foes raging against Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.7">Psa 65:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">77:19</reference>). <div eID="gen24150" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad1b56ac633a8786d68a99823aea214c51058681: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12918"/><div sID="gen24151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12918"/><hi type="bold">16. When I heard ... trembled--</hi>namely, at the judgments which God had declared (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.1-Hab.1.17">Ha 1:1-17</reference>) were to be inflicted on Judea by the Chaldeans.<div eID="gen24151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">belly--</hi>The bowels were thought by the Hebrews to be the seat of yearning compassion (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jr 31:20</reference>). Or "heard" may refer to <reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">Ha 3:2</reference>, "When I heard as to Jehovah's coming interposition for Israel against the Chaldeans being still at some distance" (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Ha 2:3</reference>); so also the voice" [Maurer].<div eID="gen24152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the voice--</hi>of the divine threatenings (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.6">Ha 1:6</reference>). The faithful tremble at the voice alone of God before He inflicts punishment. Habakkuk speaks in the person of all the faithful in Israel.<div eID="gen24153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trembled in myself--</hi>that is, I trembled all over [Grotius].<div eID="gen24154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I might rest in the day of trouble--</hi>The true and only path to rest is through such fear. Whoever is securely torpid and hardened towards God, will be tumultuously agitated in the day of affliction, and so will bring on himself a worse destruction; but he who in time meets God's wrath and trembles at His threats, prepares the best rest for himself in the day of affliction [Calvin]. Henderson translates, "Yet I shall have rest." Habakkuk thus consoling his mind, Though trembling at the calamity coming, yet I shall have rest in God (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Is 26:3</reference>). But that sentiment does not seem to be directly asserted till <reference osisRef="Hab.3.17">Ha 3:17</reference>, as the words following at the close of this verse imply.<div eID="gen24155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade--</hi>rather (as English Version is a mere truism), connected with the preceding clause, "that I might rest ... when he (the Chaldean foe) cometh up unto the people (the Jews), that he may cut them off" [Calvin]. The Hebrew for "invade" means, to rush upon, or to attack and cut off with congregated troops. <div eID="gen24156" type="x-p"/>
entries.32d00924cb1a76fe715d695da5b2802b8b813d8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12919"/><div sID="gen24157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12919"/>17. Destroy the "vines" and "fig trees" of the carnal heart, and his mirth ceases. But those who when full enjoyed God in all, when emptied can enjoy all in God. They can sit down upon the heap of ruined creature comforts, and rejoice in Him as the "God of their salvation." Running in the way of His commandments, we outrun our troubles. Thus Habakkuk, beginning his prayer with trembling, ends it with a song of triumph (<reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.4.7">Psa 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.43.3">43:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.43.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen24157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labour of the olive--</hi>that is, the fruit expected from the olive.<div eID="gen24158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fail--</hi>literally, "lie," that is, disappoint the hope (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Is 58:11</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen24159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fields--</hi>from a Hebrew root meaning "to be yellow"; as they look at harvest-time.<div eID="gen24160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meat--</hi>food, grain.<div eID="gen24161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off--</hi>that is, cease. <div eID="gen24162" type="x-p"/>
entries.1aa0677490921aaf270035902dc9dbc31b37327a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12920"/><div sID="gen24163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12920"/><hi type="bold">18. yet I will rejoice--</hi>The prophet speaks in the name of his people. <div eID="gen24163" type="x-p"/>
entries.06bb2a77edeebd35c058b5b63cdd0a25440f33d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12921"/><div sID="gen24164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12921"/><hi type="bold">19. hinds' feet ... walk upon ... high places--</hi>Habakkuk has here before his mind <reference osisRef="Ps.18.33">Psa 18:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">De 32:13</reference>. "Hinds' (gazelles') feet" imply the swiftness with which God enables him (the prophet and his people) to escape from his enemies, and return to his native land. The "high places" are called "mine," to imply that Israel shall be restored to his own land, a land of hills which are places of safety and of eminence (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.19.17">Ge 19:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.16">Mt 24:16</reference>). Probably not only the safety, but the moral elevation, of Israel above all the lands of the earth is implied (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">De 33:29</reference>).<div eID="gen24164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on my stringed instruments--</hi>neginoth. This is the prophet's direction to the precentor ("chief singer") as to how the preceding ode (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.1-Hab.3.19">Ha 3:1-19</reference>) is to be performed (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">6:1</reference>, titles). The prophet had in mind a certain form of stringed instrument adapted to certain numbers and measures. This formula at the end of the ode, directing the kind of instrument to be used, agrees with that in the beginning of it, which directs the kind of melody (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.38.20">Is 38:20</reference>). <chapter eID="Hab.3"/><div eID="gen24165" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen23983" osisID="Hab" type="book"/>

entries.d19d26324cd2749cf0b1a632e8ab28b0c964d2ae: <div eID="gen35148" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35149" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35150" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35150" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35149" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35151" type="x-p"/> The prophet, being apprised of the calamities which were to be brought on his country by the ministry of the Chaldeans, and the punishments which awaited the Chaldeans themselves, partly struck with terror, and partly revived with hope and confidence in the Divine mercy, beseeches God to hasten the redemption of his people, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.1">Hab 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">Hab 3:2</reference>. Such a petition would naturally lead his thoughts to the astonishing deliverance which God vouchsafed to the same people of old; and the inference from it was obvious, that he could with the same ease deliver their posterity now. But, hurried on by the fire and impetuosity of his spirit, he disdains to wait the process of connecting these ideas, and bounds at once into the midst of his subject: "God came from Teman," etc., <reference osisRef="Hab.3.3">Hab 3:3</reference>. He goes on to describe the majesty and might which God displayed in conducting his people to the land of promise, selecting the most remarkable circumstances, and clothing them in the most lofty language. As he goes along, his fancy becomes more glowing, till at length he is transported to the scene of action, and becomes an eyewitness of the wonders he describes. "I beheld the tents of Cushan in affliction," <reference osisRef="Hab.3.4-Hab.3.6">Hab 3:4-6</reference>. After having touched on the principal circumstances of that deliverance which he celebrates, he returns to what passed before them in Egypt; his enthusiasm having led him to begin in the midst of his subject, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.7-Hab.3.15">Hab 3:7-15</reference>. And at last he ends the hymn as he began it, with expressing his awe of the Divine judgments, and his firm trust in the mercy and goodness of God while under them; and that in terms of such singular beauty, elegance, and sublimity, as to form a to proper conclusion to this admirable piece of Divinely inspired composition, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16-Hab.3.19">Hab 3:16-19</reference>. It would seem from the title, and the note appended at the end, that it was set to music, and sung in the service of the temple. <div eID="gen35151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35152" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35153" type="x-p"/> A prayer of Habakkuk - upon Shigionoth - See the note on the title of Psalm 7 (note), where the meaning of Shiggaion is given. The Vulgate has, pro ignorantiis, for ignorances, or sins committed in ignorance; and so it is understood by the Chaldee. The Syriac has nothing but merely, A prayer of Habakkuk. And the Septuagint, instead of Shigionoth, have μετα ῳδης, with a hymn, which is copied by the Arabic. <div eID="gen35153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35154" type="x-p"/> I suspect that the title here given is of a posterior date to the prophecy. It appears to interrupt the connection between this and the termination of the preceding verse. See them together: - <reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">Hab 2:20</reference> : "But the Lord is in his holy temple:Be silent before him, all the earth. <reference osisRef="Hab.3.1">Hab 3:1</reference> : O Lord, I have heard thy speech:I have feared, O Lord, thy work.As the years approach thou hast shown;As the years approach thou makest known.In wrath thou rememberest mercy." <div eID="gen35154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35155" type="x-p"/> The prophet may here refer to the speech which God had communicated to him, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.1-Hab.1.11">Hab 1:1-11</reference>, 2:4-20, and the terror with which he was struck, because of the judgments denounced against Jerusalem. I have followed the version of Apb. Newcome in this first verse. The critical reader may consult his notes, and the various readings of Kennicott and De Rossi.
entries.512057a17e22fd7ff3b280e9ffece2780c609f22: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35156" type="x-p"/> In the midst of the years - בקרב שנים bekereb shanim, "As the years approach." The nearer the time, the clearer and fuller is the prediction; and the signs of the times show that the complete fulfillment is at hand. But as the judgments will be heavy, (and they are not greater than we deserve), yet, Lord, in the midst of wrath - infliction of punishment - remember mercy, and spare the souls that return unto thee with humiliation and prayer.
